newsitem.title: CHINA: Shanghai Lujiazui profit surges, outlook weak.
newsitem.headline: Shanghai Lujiazui profit surges, outlook weak.

text.p: Shanghai Lujiazui Finance and Trade Zone Development posted a 51.41 percent rise in 1996 net profits on Friday, but analysts said that without continued government backing its immediate prospects were poor.

Lujiazui, the key property developer in the growing financial district of Pudong east of central Shanghai, is the darling of domestic investors despite a weak property market because they assume government support will be forthcoming, the analysts said.
Lujiazui's 1996 net profit was 595.041 million yuan, compared with 393.003 yuan in 1995, based on international accounting standards, the company's annual report said.
The main source of 1996 earnings was the sale of a plot of land to Japanese developers to build the International Financial Centre Tower, planned as the world's tallest building.
The deal was finalised in 1994, signed in 1995 and booked in 1996.
Other minor sales concluded during the year turned in low prices, which analysts said bodes ill for the company's prospects for 1997 and 1998.

"Big projects like that Japanese-invested building will be difficult to get in the next few years given the office building over-supply situation in the Lujiazui area," said an analyst with a major Chinese brokerage.
Foreign brokers are almost unanimously negative on the stock due to the gloomy outlook for real estate in Pudong, with well over half the office space available there currently vacant.
But locals continue to drive the share price up.
"Local investors think the Lujiazui area (of Pudong) is like a window, so the government must support it," said an analyst with a foreign brokerage in Shanghai. "I think it's true."
Lujiazui was set up in 1992 by the Shanghai government to market a land bank in the prime Lujiazui district of Pudong, which city fathers hope will one day be the Wall Street of Asia.

The Shanghai Stock Exchange's new headquarters is due to open there in the middle of the year, and foreign banks have started to move across to Pudong from central Shanghai under pressure from the government.
The banks have been told they will only be able to do local currency business from branches established in Pudong.
Other financial exchanges and institutions are likewise being persuaded by the authorities to support Pudong.

"Lujiazui's share price represents sentiment about Shanghai," said Bruce Richardson of HG Asia. "We see improving interest in Lujiazui (and) that is a positive factor for the company. But it's difficult to say when improved interest will become income."
The company's B share, viewed as a barometer of Pudong's development potential, closed up $0.046 or 3.9 percent on Friday at $1.226.
"The company's share prices are high compared with its earnings, but investors have confidence in Pudong's future," said an analyst with a large domestic brokerage.
"They invest in Pudong's future rather than the company itself," the anlayst said.
